subjects.displayTitle: Permission for pilgrimage: longing, wisdom and care
subjects.introduction: Someone writes to ask whether they may come, and the answer that returns is at once a yes, a not yet, and a confession that the longing runs both ways. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells one friend that service to the Sacred Threshold is itself pilgrimage; Bahá’u’lláh tells another that a journey cut short by danger has been accepted as if completed. Illness, bad roads, summer heat, a family that needs its breadwinner, debts to be settled, a quarrel to be mended before setting out: these ordinary facts are treated as part of the readiness a sacred encounter asks for, much as the Qur’án joins the pilgrimage to questions of health, means and conduct [2]. The psalmist’s cry for the courts of God, where even the sparrow finds a home [1], sounds through every letter of yearning. From here the way leads toward the holy places themselves, toward the law that governs pilgrimage, toward the prayers offered for those who travel, and toward the wisdom that knows when to wait and when to go, carrying the visit home in a life.
subjects.arc: A journey of the heart → The longing to meet → Wisdom and the wider circle → Care for the traveler and those at home → Learning to wait → The service that is needed now → Companions, families and representatives → A time and a way to come → The welcome is given → Present on another’s behalf → Arrival, gratitude and return

order.why: Open with the unexpected claim that service can itself be pilgrimage, giving the administrative subject a spiritual question.
shortened: You had sought permission to come. In truth, you are worthy to don the pilgrim's garb for the sanctuary of the Desired One. However, wisdom must still be observed, and you must engage in service in that region, for service to the Sacred Threshold - meaning the diffusion of divine fragrances - is itself pilgrimage, and devotion makes the heart and soul circumambulate the gathering-place of the Concourse on High.

order.why: Place the acceptance of a journey interrupted beside the account of service as pilgrimage.
shortened: O thou who art wandering through mountain and desert! Thou didst don the pilgrim's garb for the Ka'bah of thy heart's desire, shattered the idols of self and passion, freed thyself from the bonds of comfort and ease, and set out for the dwelling-place of the Kind Friend. A barrier arose and events prevented thee, and thou wert commanded to return.
Be not disappointed, be not sorrowful, be joyous, for abundant reward is assured and the bounty bestowed upon pilgrims is ordained and destined.

shortened: O thou perfumed pilgrim! Diverse multitudes and countless throngs each year separate themselves from friend and acquaintance, kith and kin, wife and child, abandoning their familiar homeland, traversing deserts and crossing vast distances until they reach the earthly Ka'bih - an edifice metaphorically attributed to God which, through a word from the Dayspring of Revelation, has become the point of circumambulation for souls. With utmost eagerness, humility and submissiveness they circle round it, seeking acceptance at the threshold of the Almighty and hoping to attract the gaze of the Ever-Living, the All-Powerful.

shortened: Therefore, don the pilgrim's garment and set out to circumambulate the circuit of the Concourse on High. When you reach the desired land, you will witness the wisdom behind your lack of success in the previous year and will be amazed at what grace and bounty this was, and what favor and blessing it was that the pilgrimage was delayed until such days.

order.why: Close with the Báb’s account of a permission preceding the seeker’s existence, returning the reader from arrangements and dates to the mystery of nearness.

questions: How do these readings relate a journey to a sacred place with service, spiritual meeting and the orientation of the heart? What remains distinctive about physical pilgrimage?
What do the letters of postponement reveal when read beside their expressions of mutual longing? How might patience preserve a relationship and a purpose without extinguishing desire?

How do health, livelihood, family, work and the circumstances of others enter into the meaning of readiness? Which passage most challenges a separation between practical care and spiritual aspiration?
What changes when the gift brought by a pilgrim is understood as reconciliation? What might it mean to prepare relationships, as well as travel arrangements, for a sacred encounter?
How do pilgrimage by proxy, remembrance and prayer connect those who can travel with those who cannot? What do the accounts of return suggest about sharing the fruits of a visit?

What do Psalm 84 and the Qur’anic passages bring into focus, and where do the comparisons reach their limits? Which connected subject—holy places, the law of pilgrimage, prayers for pilgrims, personal instructions or wisdom—would help you pursue the question that matters most to you?

references.label: 1 · Psalm 84 · Longing for the courts of God
references.note: Psalm 84 gives longing a bodily voice: heart and flesh desire the living God, while even small birds find a home near the altar. The poem moves through travel, renewed strength, prayer and trust, and gives extraordinary value to a single day in God’s courts. Read it beside the letters that express both the pilgrim’s longing and the eagerness to welcome them. What do the images of home, threshold and journey make possible? The psalm and these letters inhabit distinct religious settings, yet each invites reflection on the relationship between a sacred place and a life oriented toward God.
references.verified: Read all twelve verses of Psalm 84 in the King James Version on Bible Gateway on 2026-10-10, including the birds, the journey through Baca, appearance in Zion, the value of a day in the courts and the closing trust.

references.label: 2 · Qur’an 2:196–197 · Provisions for a sacred journey
references.note: Read verse 196 and continue to verse 197 using the next-verse link. These verses join pilgrimage with attention to impediments, illness, available means and conduct along the way. The instruction to take provisions leads into the question of the best spiritual provision. Compare this pairing of outward preparation and inward discipline with the letters about comfortable travel, fulfilled responsibilities, reconciliation and wisdom. The Islamic ritual provisions and the individual permissions in this compilation serve different purposes; the comparison asks how practical care and spiritual intention can belong to the same journey.
